content.thinking: I should keep root cause unconfirmed—the deploy correlation is only a leading hypothesis, not established fact. For the executive summary, I want to avoid naming specific components and instead describe the shop service as slow/timing out for at least four minutes and still ongoing as of the last data point, with the automated rollback having failed and the issue unresolved.

assumptions: That the deployment at 23:26:00Z is related to the failure at all — this rests only on the coincidence of timing, not on inspection of what the revision changed.

That the onset was 23:26 — this is the earliest minute in the four-minute metrics window that was read, so the fault may have begun earlier and the stated duration is a floor rather than a measurement.
That the two batches of log lines retrieved (33-minute and 9-minute windows) are the same six lines repeated, not twelve distinct events; they name no endpoint, dependency or error detail.
That the service remained impaired after the last metric read — no recovery was observed, but no recovery check was performed either.
That flag changes are ruled out: the flag provider reported no recent changes, which was checked.
The alternative explanation of an unresponsive downstream dependency was never tested; no dependency could be identified from the logs retrieved.
input.executive_summary: Shortly before midnight UTC on 22 September 2026, an internal service began responding very slowly and then failing outright: requests that normally completed in a fifth of a second were taking five seconds and then timing out. Anyone depending on that service during the window would have seen slow or failed requests. The fault began at 23:26 UTC and was still present in the last minute of data we could read, so we know it lasted at least a few minutes but we do not know when — or whether — it ended; how many requests failed is also unknown, because the metrics needed to measure that could not be retrieved. Automated triage picked up the alert within seconds, noted that a change to the service's deployment settings had gone out in the exact minute the trouble started, and attempted to undo that change. The undo could not be performed — the service had no earlier version to fall back to — so the incident was escalated to on-call engineers while still unresolved. No mitigation was successfully applied by the automated system.
input.root_cause: Not established. The only evidence linking cause to effect is timing: a deployment from the io-shop k8s-configs (configuration) repository landed at revision 9f4c1e7b2a3d5c8e1f0b6a4d2c9e7b5a3f1d8c6e in the same minute as the onset (23:26:00Z), after which p95 latency climbed monotonically from a 220ms baseline to a 5000ms timeout ceiling while traffic and memory stayed flat — a pattern equally consistent with a bad config value, a code-bearing release, or an unresponsive downstream dependency. The change record does not say what the revision altered and no log line names an endpoint or dependency, so the leading hypothesis (a bad configuration value) remains a correlation, not a confirmed cause.
